### ★09-15 single.md S1 landed: decode 68.9 → 58.7 ms(14.5 → 17.0 t/s), the long tail disappears★

**The disease** (newly dug out from the 09-15 per-kernel timeline, the ledger now baked into `d0a_decode_profile.sh ③`): the expert kernel gateup's per-layer µs is
`235 235 … 235 **2331** 217 **3591 4524 1136**` —— L35/L37/L38/L39 are 10~20× other layers, and the first step is 38 ms for the whole kernel.
True cause: `cuda_model_cache_limit_bytes()`'s budget = physical memory − **24 GiB headroom** = 97.7 GiB, while the model is 109.79 GiB
⇒ about 12 GiB (exactly the last few layers' expert blobs) does not fit into the device copy, and `ds4_gpu_cache_model_range` **silently** falls back to
cudaHostRegister mapping; those pages get reclaimed constantly by kswapd on a 130 GB machine, and every step page-faults back in from NVMe.
★Not one word of this is visible in the startup log —— this is the reason this bug lived until today.★

**Three cuts** (all in S1):
1. Headroom **24 → 8 GiB** (segments copied into the device immediately `MADV_DONTNEED`, the page cache carries no load at all; 8 GiB covers
   KV@32k 2.4 + scratch 2 + CUDA context 1.5 + a 2 buffer).
2. A third tier added to load priority: **main backbone 0 > main expert blob 1 > `mtp.*` three towers 2**. The three towers' 7.3 GiB have neither
   `_exps.` nor `_exps_vq.` in their names, so they were scored prio 0 and loaded first, competing with the backbone, pushing out the last few layers' blobs ——
   while with speculation off these 7.3 GiB are never read even once.
3. **Reconciliation print + a load-time memory floor gate**: startup prints "loaded into device x / via host mapping y", and y>0 raises a loud warning; the load loop checks
   `/proc/meminfo MemAvailable` per segment and stops when it drops below **12 GB** (measured trough after loading 10.8 GB, floor 10 GB —— 09-08 hit
   swap at 5 GB and decode went 21.6 → 12.5). ★The reconciliation's denominator must be "everything that should be loaded", not "what happened to get loaded this time", the latter is always 0★ (the first version got this wrong).

**Readings** (same file native 117.9 GB, `d0a_decode_profile.sh 32` median formulation):

| | median ms | t/s | max ms | expert kernel Max | cache reconciliation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Before S1 | 68.9 | 14.5 | 96.8 | 49.1 ms | (none) |
| **After S1** | **58.7** | **17.04** | 62.3 | **1.69 ms** | loaded 106.51 GiB / mapped 3.28 GiB (all three towers, decode does not read them) |

Temp-0 output is verbatim unchanged (only "where the bytes live" was changed, no operator touched). In the per-layer milliseconds, L35~L39 are now the same 1.4~1.5 ms as other layers.

### 09-15 single.md S3/S4 landed: decode 58.7 → 56.2 ms, long context −21%, prefill +14% along the way

**S4 decode attention split-K** (new artifact `src/cuda/cuda_v41_attn_split.inc.cu`): at decode the original kernel's grid is only
(n_tok=1, 8 head groups) = **8 blocks**, 40 of 48 SMs idle, chewing the keys in series (measured 5.3 µs/key). Changed to split by key range
(grid = key segment × head group), each segment emits a local (max,sum,acc), then one launch merges them in **fixed segment-number order** (no atomic add —— that would make the same
input give two different runs). ★Invisible at short context★: at 32 steps the visible keys are only ~70, below the 128 split threshold, so it takes the original kernel;
**under a 12464 token prompt 268.2 → 211.3 ms(−21%)**, generated text not one word off.

**S3 mHC kernel merging + sinkhorn parallelism**:
- The merge itself (hc_split + hc_pre + rms_norm in one launch) **is only a tie** —— the 160 launches saved are eaten back by "hc_pre shrinking from
  grid(20, n_tok) to grid(n_tok)".
- The real win is **changing the 20 rounds of sinkhorn from serial on thread 0 to one thread per element**: that launch measured 35 µs × 80 half-layers =
  2.8 ms/step, while what it computes is merely a 4×4 matrix. **58.7 → 56.2 ms(17.04 → 17.81 t/s)**.
  The row/column sums are accumulated in ascending order serially **within the thread** ⇒ element-for-element the same order as the serial version, ★numerically bit-identical★ (a shfl tree reduction would not be).
- ★A collision hit★: `if (act) { … __syncthreads(); } else __syncthreads();` —— it looks like both sides reach the barrier,
  but they are actually **two different barrier points**, the kernel hangs outright, the GPU does not return, the process needs kill -9. The correct shape is
  "compute → all sync → write → all sync", barriers always outside the branches.

**S2 expert kernel: all three hypotheses negative** (all same-machine-state A/B, archived in code comments)
| What was tried | reading | why |
|---|---:|---|
| Codebook changed to global `__ldg` (drop shared, open up occupancy) | 58.7 → **71.0(21% slower)** | the inner loop randomly gathers 640 times 16 B per row, even L2 hits cannot carry it; the shared version is "move 64 KB once, reused by 64 rows" |
| Activation x into shared (saves re-reading 20 KB per row) | 59.6(tie) | same origin as the gemv attempt: L1 already catches it, an extra write + an extra sync is paid |
| Codebook 20 B stride to remove bank conflicts | 59.9(tie) | 20 B is not a multiple of 8 ⇒ uint2 reads misalign and crash, falling back to 4 uint reads, whose extra instructions eat the conflict savings |
⇒ The expert kernel's bottleneck is neither occupancy, nor activation re-read, nor shared banks. ITERS re-swept (after the long tail was fixed): 2 = 58.7 < 4 = 59.8 < 8 = 63.0, keep 2.
★S2④ "merge gate/up/down into one kernel" does not hold structurally★: down needs the whole row h(2304), while gateup produces only 64 rows per block —— that item in single.md was written optimistically.

**Prefill benefits in step** (same native file, `prefill_2048_ruler.sh` 2048 token / chunk 512):
| | seconds | t/s | PPL |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| C1a record (before S1) | 23.0~24.0 | ~87 | 15.6714 |
| **After S1+S3+S4** | **20.5~20.6** | **99.4~99.9** | **15.6714(bit-identical, reproduced twice)** |

★An operational lesson★: using `git checkout <file>` mid-way to roll back an A/B lost **109 lines of earlier rounds' uncommitted work**
(GEMV template specialization / lane 4-byte layout / ksplit 32768 target) along with it, and they had to be restored line by line from the session log.
**An A/B rollback must use "change back those lines", not git checkout —— this repo's working tree permanently carries uncommitted changes.**

### ★09-16 single.md S5 final verdict: in-kernel decode optimization is at its end (56.0 ms / 17.8 t/s), the wall is the on-disk format★

All five of S5's cuts fall inside the noise (±1 ms, same-machine-state median):
| What was tried | reading | |
|---|---:|---|
| Inner loop unrolled by two groups (raise ILP, two groups of weight loads in flight in parallel) | 55.9 | the compiler already unrolled it |
| Remove the inner `v41_bf16r` (the activation is already on the bf16 grid before entering the kernel, re-rounding is identity) | 56.0 | instructions are not the bottleneck; but keep this cut (bit-identical + 32 fewer ALU ops per round) |
| ksplit target 32768 → 8192 | **55.7~56.3** | keep: large matrices return to rpb=8, activation reused 8× |
| ksplit target → 4096 | 57.0 | small matrices do not have enough warps to cover latency, back out |

★The explanation ncu gives (the most valuable number this round)★: `v41_fp4x32_gemv_kernel`'s
**l1tex averages 24.92 sectors/request** (ideal 4). Three kernels on the same board for comparison:

| Kernel | on-disk format | bandwidth | share of the wall |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| engram wkv `fp8blk_gemv` | **planar** (one e4m3 plane + one scale plane) | **214 GB/s** | **89%** |
| Backbone `fp4x32_gemv` | **interleaved** (16 B nibble + 1 B scale, stride **17 B**) | 165 | 69% |
| Expert `vq_gateup/down` | bitstream + one 16 B codebook lookup per 8 weights | 110 | 46% |

⇒ **The bandwidth of the two big kernels (66% of decode) is set by the on-disk format, not the kernel shape**. The 17 B stride makes every block unaligned;
S2's three cuts (global codebook/activation into shared/bank stride) and S5's five all turn inside the kernel, hence all negative —— it is not that the right move was not found,
it is that the move was made in the wrong place.

**There are only two next steps, both requiring a format change (converter + re-convert + five-metric gate, needs the user's nod)**:
- A. fp4x32 to planar (one nibble plane + one ue8m0 scale plane): numerically bit-identical, judged against the engram row it could reach 165 → 200+,
  GEMV 22.9 → ≈18 ms, full step ≈51 ms(19.6 t/s).
- B. The expert VQ's codebook lookup is VQ's inherent cost; to touch it means changing the quantization format itself —— that is a quality-line decision.

**Today's running total** (same native file, same machine state): decode **68.9 → 56.0 ms(14.5 → 17.8 t/s, +23%)**;
long context 12k decode **268 → 211 ms(−21%)**; prefill CED **440.9 t/s** (scoring ruler 99.9 t/s, PPL 15.6714 bit-identical over two runs).

### ★09-16 S6 changing target: launch is not the bottleneck, "the GPU waiting for the host" is —— the engram thread pool saves 1.8 ms (54.2 ms / 18.45 t/s)★

The plan was for CUDA graph to pull in that 5 ms launch gap. **First the premise was measured, and the premise does not hold**:
`cudaLaunchKernel` 47443 launches per full step take only **3.4 ms of CPU time**, while the GPU kernels are busy 51 ms —— the host launches 10× faster than the GPU,
so what graph could save was already overlapped away. The 5 ms gap is **the GPU waiting at a few specific points for the host**.

Splitting the gaps by "which kernel is before and after" (awk over the nsys timeline, 21 steps accumulated):

| Location | per step | what it is |
|---|---:|---|
| **H2D → embed** | **2.59 ms** | `v41_engram_prefetch` does `pthread_create` **48 threads** every step + 48 `posix_memalign` + 3 malloc |
| D2H → next step's H2D | 0.87 ms | host-side loop (emit / next-step preparation / 3 **synchronous** cudaMemcpy) |
| engram layer hc_post → H2D | 0.47 ms | genuinely waiting for pread to complete |

★The first item is pure waste★: at decode n=1 the row fetch task is exactly 2 layers × 24 rows = 48 units, so the thread count maxes out at 48, while the actual IO
is only 48 aligned 4 KB reads (parallel on NVMe, a few hundred microseconds) —— the overhead is all in spawning threads. Changed to a **resident thread pool**
(`src/core/core_v41_epool.c`, threads spawned once and never dispersed, each step only fills parameters + broadcasts a condition variable; the bounce landing point is also allocated only once):

| | median ms | t/s |
|---|---:|---:|
| S5 close-out | 56.0 | 17.86 |
| **+ engram resident thread pool** | **54.2** | **18.45** |

The concurrency structure is untouched (still one thread per row, each writing its own segment) ⇒ it neither introduces nor fixes E0's "four runs at temp 0 give four PPLs".
All gates green: prefill 2048 PPL **15.6714 bit-identical over two runs**; prefill CED **442.5 t/s**; temp-0 generated text verbatim unchanged; linecount green.

**Today's running total**: decode **68.9 → 54.2 ms(14.5 → 18.45 t/s, +27%)**; long context 12k **268 → 211 ms(−21%)**;
prefill CED **442.5 t/s**; PPL not moved by one byte.

### ★★09-16 single-1.md review: single.md aimed at the wrong target —— the real wall is the long-context indexer path, 12k decode 4.51 → 12.60 t/s★★

The user asked to "analyze why single.md is far short of expectations, is it a plan problem or a hidden bug", the review's conclusion lands in `single-1.md`. **Both are true**.

**One, the ruler itself was wrong**: all of single.md measures decode with a **3 token prompt**, yielding 54.2 ms/step = 18.45 t/s.
The same binary under a **12464 token prompt** is **222 ms/step = 4.51 t/s**. The 40 t/s the user wants is the number in real conversation,
and the extra 157 ms there was never itemized by anyone (09-15's S4 gave only the total 268 → 211).

**Two, the true body of those 157 ms** (`d0a_decode_profile.sh`'s newly extended 4th parameter = long prompt, per-kernel table):

| Kernel | ms/step | launches/step | grid |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `v41_indexer_score_kernel` | **80.33** | 8 | **(1,1)** |
| `v41_candidate_kernel` | **46.39** | 1 | **(1,1)** |
| `v41_topk_kernel` | 5.89 | 8 | **(1,1)** |
| Backbone GEMV | 22.11 | 329 | |
| Attention split / expert | 10.75 / 14.5 | 40 / 80 | |

**The indexer trio is 132.6 ms = 66% of the full step, and all three kernels' grid is one block (1 of 48 SMs used)**.
The engine's per-layer milliseconds point to the same place: of the 40 layers 36 are 1.3 ms each, while **L20 (the candidate source layer) is 60.6 ms for one layer**, and the other 4 indexer source layers are 14.7 each.
`v41_candidate_kernel`'s disease is exactly the same as the surgery done on the topk kernel on 09-14 (thread 0 serial O(kk×nb), 2.4 million rounds at 12k), **that time this kernel was missed**.

**Three, two cuts landed (both bit-identical: only "who computes" and "how to select" changed)**:
- The scoring kernel's grid (n_tok) → (n_tok, group blocks), 8 groups per block ⇒ **80.33 → 0.90 ms**.
- The candidate-block kernel: when kk ≥ nb select all (equivalent to the original round-by-round completion of all non -inf blocks), when kk < nb a parallel radix select sets the threshold +
  ties are filled in ascending block number ⇒ **46.39 → drops out of the top 18**.
- Attention split threshold **128 → 16** + segment length adapted to the key count (target 6 segments per head group = 48 blocks): short context used to fall back
  to the 8-block original kernel because visible keys ~70 < 128, **4.45 → 1.40 ms/step**.

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| 12464 token context decode | 222 ms / **4.51 t/s** | **79 ms / 12.60 t/s(2.8×)** |
| 3 token context decode | 54.6 ms / 18.30 t/s | **52.7 ms / 18.98 t/s** |

**Four, two cuts negative, archived in code comments** (both attributed via the per-kernel table, not by A/B guessing):
| What was tried | basis | reading | why negative |
|---|---|---:|---|
| GEMV 8 lanes per block + one float4 activation | SASS: the activation compiles into 8 scalar `LDG.E.CONSTANT`, one instruction spreading 32 lanes over 1024 B ⇒ 32 sectors/request | 20.83 → **22.75** | a round drops from 8 blocks to 4, the loop iterations double; the sectors saved were **hitting L1** anyway |
| VQ bitstream aligned read + funnelshift | SASS: the bitstream's 4 B memcpy compiles into **4 `LDG.E.U8`** | 14.04 → **18.81** | the tail needs a boundary check ⇒ one more three-way branch in the hot loop; those 4 byte reads already fell in the same 32 B sector |

★These two cuts, together with 09-16 S2/S5's eight, show the same thing★: **ncu's "sectors/request" and SASS's instruction count are both L1-side quantities,
and their looking ugly does not mean the warp is waiting on DRAM**. To touch these two kernels, first ask `smsp__warp_issue_stalled_{long_scoreboard,mio_throttle,lg_throttle}`.

**Five, two ruler traps fixed along the way**:
- `d0a_decode_profile.sh`'s `nsys stats` reused the old sqlite and only deleted it before ③, while ②'s kern_sum/api_sum kept reading the **previous**

**Six, the composition of a 67 ms step at 12k now**: GEMV 21.9 / expert 14.3 / attention split 10.5 / **topk 5.9** / mHC etc. 4 / gaps 4.7.
`v41_topk_kernel` rises to fourth, it too is one block scanning 12480 groups —— the next cut.

### ★09-16 decode.md case opened: rewriting the decode architecture per the official V4.1 design (report §2.2~2.4/§3.2 + model.py item-by-item comparison)★

User order "design the decode architecture per the official document" ⇒ new file `decode.md` (the report PDF is also fetched back into `docs/`). **Conclusion: structurally the engine is already the official one
(CED/CSA2 three modes/candidate pool/single-pass mHC/engram/DSpark all wired up from metadata), but in shape it is not** —— each layer ≈35 kernel launches (the official Reuse layer 11),
all caches f32 (official FP4/FP8, bytes 7×), the window moved twice per layer per step, 3 synchronous host copies per step, the n>1 verification batch takes a different set of kernels.

★**First correct an error of my own**★: the first version of decode.md gave a "target ms" table (12k 79 → 44 ms / 23 t/s), and the user called it out on the spot,
**"is this guessed blindly with no basis"**. On review it is true: only two items in the table had a basis (GEMV planar format and top-k multi-block; ncu sectors + same-shape surgery),
mHC kernel merging and small-kernel fusion both **have counter-evidence** (09-16 S3/S5 measured "a tie"), and the attention item was pure speculation. The whole column of target numbers has been deleted, changed to marking each item
"was there a basis beforehand", and the total is not forecast. **While at it, make the precision point clear**: the official original model FP8 backbone + FP4 expert ≈12 GB/token, on this
240 GB/s board the wall is only 20 t/s; ours, fp4x32 + VQ 1.5 bpw, is 6.0 GB, **half the original model's weight** —— what can be borrowed from the official side is
the mechanism of kernel stream/cache format/prefetch and scheduling, **not one speed number can be borrowed** (the official 11 kernels are counted on their tensor core + FP8 activation).

### ★★09-16 decode.md D1 landed: cache in official format + window as a ring —— real 12k scenario 67.9 → 61.7 ms(14.75 → 16.21 t/s)★★

★The ruler changed★ (user order "no short prompts, real scenarios only"): the whole 3 token short-prompt family is retired, gates and speeds are all on 2K / 12k real English prompts.

**Four changes** (all only changing "where things live, who computes", touching no values):

1. **SWA window becomes a ring** (official `window_kv_cache[start_pos % win]`): position a always lives in cell a % 128. It used to be a sorted
   linear buffer, each step shifting the whole range one row left = two 256 KB copies per layer, 40 layers moving 20 MB per step for nothing. New artifact `src/cuda/cuda_kv_ring.inc.cu`
   (three small kernels: commit/snapshot/rollback) + `v41_win_row` row-number mapping (the draft towers still take the linear segment, ring=0 passed —— they hold the main_x projection and are fully visible within the block).
2. **Speculative rollback 10.5 MB → 0.5 MB**: this batch's n rows **do not enter the ring first**, they stay in the buffer's [window, window+n) segment, and attention reads there by absolute position;
   only once how many positions are accepted is confirmed are that many rows committed. So a rejected draft position never pollutes history, and rollback only restores "the few cells overwritten at commit".
3. **Main KV / index K packed per the official scheme** (new artifact `src/cuda/cuda_kv_pack.inc.cu`): main KV 512-dim FP4 + one E4M3 scale per 16
   = **288 B/group** (was 2048); index K 128-dim FP4 + one E8M0 per 32 = 68 B, padded to **72 B/group** (was 512) for alignment.
   ★This is not a precision drop★: the values were already quantized by act_quant (each number has only 16 possible values), they were merely stored at 4 B each. Storage packs (nibble, scale),
   and reading back computes bf16(nibble×scale) —— exactly the number act_quant's last line wrote back, **bit-identical**.
   Two encoders `ds4_e8m0_f32_to_byte`/`ds4_e4m3fn_f32_to_byte` go into `src/common/ds4_fp8.h` (format primitives allowed in only one copy).
   1M cache ledger: 6.4 GB → **0.9 GB**, matching the official 890 B/token (speed.md §5.2's memory table only holds now).
4. The index keys are **unpacked into registers first** before entering the 32-head loop (the f32 version previously also re-read 32 times, caught by L1).

**Readings** (median of two runs, same machine state, `--no-dspark`):

| prompt | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2K English | 60.2 / 60.2 ms = 16.61 t/s | 61.5 / 61.0 ms = **16.34**(2% slower) |
| 12k English | 67.8 / 68.0 ms = 14.75 t/s | 61.6 / 61.8 ms = **16.21 t/s(+9.9%)** |

★**The two directions are opposite, and correct**★: packing saves "bytes of reading compressed keys", and this grows with context —— at 12k each step reads 512 top-k groups,
each group read once by each of 8 head groups, f32 is 335 MB/step, FP4 drops to 47 MB, outweighing the unpacking's extra ALU; at 2K there are few visible groups and the bytes saved
do not pay for unpacking, a net 1 ms loss. **The longer the context the more it earns**, and what the user wants is exactly real conversation.

**All gates green** (`speed-bench/d1_kv_ring_gate.sh`, against the pre-change binary): the three scenarios 2K pure decode / 12k / 2K speculative are **byte-identical**,
the speculative acceptance-rate histogram is exactly the same (31 rounds 1.03/5). The gate is byte-identity, not NLL —— this cut only changes "which row a key lives in, how many bytes store it",
it is numerically identical, one differing byte means the mapping is wrong and it must not be let through as noise.

**One explicit deferral**: the SWA window is **not packed**. It is 2.6 MB in total, worth only 0.25 ms at 12k, and packing would drag the draft-tower path in with it —— not worth it.

★Line-count warning★: `cuda_v41_2.inc.cu` is already at **498 lines** (guard 500), the next cut touching it must split it first.

### 09-16 decode.md D2: mHC three launches merged + compressed-key scale pre-solved (byte-identical, 12k 61.7 → 61.2 ms)

1. **Three launches of mix merged into one** (`cuda_v41_hc.inc.cu` gains `v41_hc_mix_fused_kernel`): previously three kernels ①row_rsqrt ②f32 GEMV ③scale_rows.
   ①'s grid is just n_tok —— **at decode only 1 block**, reading 82 KB takes 13.4 µs (= 6 GB/s), once per half-layer × 40 layers = 80 launches/step ≈ 1.1 ms of pure latency.

   —— a different formulation is a different sum, and one pass through sinkhorn amplifies it into different mixing coefficients.
2. **The compressed key's 32 scales are solved once per row** (`v41_ckv_get_s`): after D1c's packing, moving one 512-dim row in attention required calling 512 times

   **This cut pulled back D1c's −2% regression at 2K** (2K 61.2 → 60.0).
3. In passing: `cuda_v41_2.inc.cu` at 501 lines broke the guard ⇒ the act_quant family moved into `cuda_kv_pack.inc.cu` (it was the same matter anyway: the same

### ★★09-16 decode.md D2 main cut: decode attention onto tensor cores —— 12k 61.2 → 51.0 ms(16.34 → 19.61 t/s, +20%)★★

After excluding occupancy and bytes, the only suspect left is **instruction count**: the scalar version pays one 5-shfl warp reduction per (key, head)
computed to buy 16 FMAs, plus expf and two bf16 roundings. This is the same thing diagnosed on 09-15 segment 4 when writing the mma version for **prefill**
(that prefill was 1.76×) —— the decode path did not follow at the time, because the mma version's grid is (n_tok, head group), and n_tok=1 gives only 4 blocks.

**Landed** (new artifact `src/cuda/cuda_v41_attn_mma_decode.inc.cu`, 150 lines): the mma version **+ split by key range**, same skeleton as the scalar split ——
grid (key segment, 16 heads per group), each block does the full two-pass online softmax on its own key segment, emitting a local (max, sum, acc),
then hands it to the **existing** `v41_sparse_attn_merge_kernel` to merge in fixed segment-number order. For one query, S = Q[64×512]·Kᵀ[512×nkeys]
is a real GEMM to begin with, and this is the shape it should have. gather/scores **directly reuse prefill's two device functions**, no second copy written
—— a second copy would sooner or later drift from prefill's (invalid topk slots' "zero out + push -inf" omit either and it silently goes astray).

| | 2K | 12k |
|---|---:|---:|
| D2 scalar version | 60.0 ms / 16.67 t/s | 61.2 ms / 16.34 t/s |
| **Decode tensor-core version** | **49.9 ms / 20.04 t/s** | **51.0 ms / 19.61 t/s** |

★Not byte-identical★ (the tensor-core accumulation order + the segmented online softmax grouping both changed, the same rule as 09-15 segment 4) ⇒ the gate uses the quality ruler:

### ★★09-16 The true cause of speculative decoding: not the acceptance rate, but "verifying 4 positions ≈ verifying 4 times"★★

After a whole day of staring at the acceptance rate (M6 drafter alignment) and a negative verdict, the first time a **wall-clock ledger** was added for one speculative round (core_v41_api.c), 12k real prompt:

```
一轮 188.3 ms = 草稿 39.7 + 快照回滚 0.2 + 验证 147.7 + argmax 0.7
产出 1.96 token ⇒ 96.1 ms/token   (纯解码 52 ms/token)
```

**Verifying 4 tokens costs 147.7 ms, while a single-token forward takes only 52 ms.** Speculative decoding's entire premise is "the backbone weights are shared,
verifying 1+k positions is about equal to verifying 1 position", and this premise **does not hold** in our shape.

The same ruler measures the expert kernel (the d0a per-kernel table gives n=1, the same batch's A/B gives n=4):

| | n=1 | n=4 | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Expert VQ kernel | 0.356 ms/layer | 1.283 ms/layer | **3.6×** |

Nearly linear ⇒ the weights are not amortized at all. **No acceptance rate, however high, can save it**: one round's bytes 12.2 GB ÷ 1.96 token = 6.2 GB/token,
more than pure decode's 6.0. This is the root of all three generations of speculation failing, the previous three rounds (including M6) all pushed on the wrong end.

**Drafter byte ledger** (engine self-reported, `v41_draft_byte_report`): dense three towers 0.26 GB + activated experts 0.79 + exit head/main_proj 0.37
= **1.41 GB/chunk**, yet it takes 38.7 ms —— at the decode path's effective bandwidth (115 GB/s) it should be only 12 ms, **3.2× slower**, the three towers' dozens of kernels each computing only 5 rows,
it is launch overhead not bytes.

### ★09-16 M3 negative-verdict archive: verify batch deduplicated by expert —— 41% fewer bytes, slower instead★

The evidence looked solid: the newly added `[moe-uniq]` line of `--v41-prof` measured that in a 3-row batch, of the 24 (token, expert) pairs only **14.2 = 59%** are unique experts,
four tenths of the expert reads are pure duplication (the active VQ path is `np = n_tok × top8` pairs, one block per pair, each reading on its own).
Wrote a dedup kernel (one block handles one expert, the bitstream and the codebook are traversed once, each token in the pair group accumulates one dot product; only "which block computes which pair" is changed,
h/partial still land by pair ⇒ bit-identical by design).

**Same-batch A/B** (the same x/sel issued back to back + CUDA events; running the whole stretch in two separate passes to compare wall clock is not comparable —— once the output changes, the following tokens
and the selected experts all change):

| How many per group | vs per-pair |
|---|---:|
| 2 | 1.7% slower |
| 4 | 7.1% slower |

The more dedup, the slower, monotonically. **Real cause**: the bulk of this kernel is the **reuse of activations in L1**, not reading weights from DRAM. The codebook takes 64 KB of shared,
leaving only ~64 KB of L1; the per-pair path has one block touching just one activation (20 KB), and 63 of 64 rows hit in L1. Grouping 4 ⇒ working set 80 KB
does not fit ⇒ every row goes back to L2 to refetch. **Same root** as those 09-15/09-16 cuts (activations into shared 66% slower, 8-lane tiling 9% slower).

A pit hit midway is worth recording: the activation pointer's `pair/K` was written inside the inner loop = one runtime integer division per index, thousands per row,
**so the first version was 23% slower**, and it nearly got the whole path condemned on that basis; hoisting it out of the loop revealed the real 1.7%.
Also, 1024 threads × 64 registers already saturate the whole SM's register file; two more pointers and it is `too many resources requested`.

The code was withdrawn (the archive comment stays in `v41_vq_fused_moe` in `cuda_v41_4.inc.cu`); the `[moe-uniq]` probe and the one-round wall-clock breakdown are kept.

| Kernel | ms/step | bytes/token | effective bandwidth | share of the 240 GB/s wall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| backbone fp4x32 GEMV | 21.4 | 3.82 GB | 178 GB/s | 74% |
| expert VQ (gateup+down) | 14.2 | 1.61 GB | **113 GB/s** | **47%** |
| mHC family | 4.1 | — | non-byte work | — |
| attention (tensor-core version + merge) | 2.3 | — | non-byte work | — |
| rest + launch gaps | ~10 | — | — | — |
| **total** | **52 ms** | 6.0 GB | 115 GB/s | 48% |

★The ordering of the next cut is set by this table★: ① expert kernel 113 → 178 GB/s (catching up with the backbone kernel) is worth 5.2 ms; ② backbone kernel 178 → 240 is worth 5.5 ms;
③ that ~10 ms of non-byte work (mHC/attention/launch) is the third block. Getting all three = 32.6 ms = 30.7 t/s.
**Speculative decoding is not worth further investment until the "verify does not amortize" item is cured.**

### ★★09-16 Striking the expert kernel: the culprit is how the activations are read, not the weights —— two cuts −3.10 ms/step, bit-identical throughout★★

The trigger was re-prioritizing after the speculative negative verdict (see the bandwidth checkup table in the previous entry): the expert VQ kernel only reached 47% of the wall, the item furthest from it.
Per the discipline hard-coded in the repo, **first ask ncu where the warp stalls**, do not change code directly —— the first three cuts were all negative values bought by skipping this step.

**What ncu said** (one launch of `v41_vq_gateup_kernel` = one layer):

```
wavefront 18.24 M   全局 load 扇区 42.0 M (= 1.34 GB)   扇区/请求 10.99
一层的 warp 轮数 = 2048 行 × 8 对 × 2 矩阵 × 20 轮 = 655,360
⇒ 每轮 27.8 个 wavefront / 64 个扇区 = 2048 B
```

The weights this layer actually needs to read are only 31.5 MB, yet the sector traffic is 1.34 GB —— **a 43× amplification**. That 2048 B/round is **all activation**:
each lane needs 8 f32 = 32 B, there is no 32 B load instruction, so it is split into two float4; within each, the 32 lanes' addresses are 32 B apart,
**one instruction spreads out 1024 B to use only 512 B**. The weight bitstream is only 48 B per round. ★The bottleneck is the activation, not the weights.★

**Cut ①: store the expert kernel's activations as bf16** (`v41_vq_dot8` in `cuda_vq_decode.inc.cu`).
8 elements are exactly 16 B contiguous ⇒ one uint4, and the 32 lanes' combined 512 B is fully used. The gateup h output is also written directly as bf16.
★The basis for bit-identical is not "it ran and changed nothing"★: the activations are already on the bf16 grid, so restoring with zero padding is an identity transform. The newly added watchdog
`[vq-grid]` (--v41-prof) measured **elements off the grid 0 / 1,228,800** —— that is harder than hashing the output; identical hashes only prove this prompt did not expose it.

**Cut ②: read the backbone GEMV's activations as two float4** (`V41_GEMV_BLK` in `cuda_v41_4.inc.cu`).
The same disease, more severe: one warp covers 8 blocks per round = 256 floats = **1024 B that is already contiguous**, exactly 32 B per lane,
a perfectly coalesced shape; but written as `for j<8: xt[j]` the compiler cannot prove alignment and emits **8 scalar LDG.E.CONSTANT = 64 wavefronts**.
Two float4 ⇒ 16. ★The difference from that 09-16 negative-verdict archive★: that one changed "which lane handles which block", doubling the loop round count for 9% slower;
this time the lane assignment is not changed by a single word, only the read method.

| Kernel (12k real prompt, nsys per-kernel table) | before | now |
|---|---:|---:|
| backbone fp4x32 GEMV | 21.42 | **19.27** (−10.0%) |
| expert VQ gateup | 9.24 | **8.29** (−10.3%) |
| expert VQ down | 4.99 | **4.99** |
| three-item total | 35.65 | **32.55(−3.10 ms/step)** |

End to end (temp 0, `--no-dspark`): 2K **20.16 t/s** / 12k **20.09 t/s** (previously 19.61).
Gate: **byte-identical** to the pre-change binary ✓ (64 tokens each for the two contexts).

**★The pit hit, worth more than the result★**: the first version of the float4 cut merged the eight accumulations into one expression
`acc += w0x0 + w1x1 + ... + w7x7`. `--use_fast_math` lets the compiler evaluate the right-hand side as an addition tree and then fold it into acc,
**so the accumulation order changes** —— the output starts diverging around the 100th character, and **reads perfectly fluently**, only a byte-by-byte comparison catches it.
Reverting to eight independent `acc +=` matched, and was faster (19.91 → 19.27).
⇒ From now on, when changing the read method in this kind of hot loop, "same values" is not enough, **how the additions associate must also match to the word**.

### ★09-16 negative-verdict archive: bitstream "32 lanes cooperate to read + shfl distribute" (third same-root negative verdict)★

The evidence is the hardest of the three: one round of 32 indices × nbit bits = **exactly nbit aligned 32-bit words** (always divides evenly), so let
lane 0..nbit-1 each read one word (combined into a single 48 B request), broadcast to the whole warp, each funnel-shifting out its own 12 bits,
memory instructions per round **4 LDG.E.U8 → 1 LDG.E.32**, and bit-identical.
Same ruler, measured separately from cut ①: **gateup 8.37 → 8.78 (+4.9%) / down 4.98 → 6.03 (+21%)**, rolled back.
Why: those 4 byte reads fall in the same 32 B sector, L1 supplies them in one go, they are **not waiting on memory at all**; what was bought is
a dependency chain of "load → two shfl → funnel-shift", and shfl requires whole-warp alignment, which also cuts off the parallelism of lanes fetching their own data.
Together with the other two (09-16 "two aligned reads + funnel-shift" 32% slower, "8 lanes per block + float4" 9% slower):
**the bitstream read method is not this kernel's bottleneck, do not touch it again.**

### ★★09-16 night M1′ close-out: same-track is green —— the true cause is "the attention segment length swallowed the batch size", the fix is to compute by each query's own position★★

**The disease**: the decode tensor-core attention cuts the keys into segments for online softmax, and the segment length was written as `24 / n_tok` segments —— the same query at the same position,
pure decode cuts 20 segments, the verify batch 10, **different groupings ⇒ different accumulation order ⇒ tokens near a tie flip**. All of speculation's legitimacy
rests on "saves time only, does not change the output"; once that is broken, no later speed number can be judged.

**Four attempts, the first three all wrong (what is valuable is why they were wrong)**:

| How the segment length is set | same-track | pure decode vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| `ceil(nkeys / (24/n_tok))` (original) | ✗ 2K diverges at byte 152 | — |
| hard-coded 64 / 32 / 16 | ✓ | **4~6% slower** (2K 20.14 → 19.16 / 18.61) |
| computed from the position of **this batch's first** query | ✗ still diverges | byte-identical |
| ★computed from **each query's own absolute position** (moved into the kernel)★ | **✓** | **byte-identical** |

★Why a constant does not work★: this model's layers fall into two classes —— layers with a large compression ratio have only a hundred-odd visible keys (window 128 + that layer's top-k),
and need 16 keys per segment to cut enough blocks to fill the 48 SMs; key-heavy layers (2K ≈588, 12k 640) need 32, and a shorter segment just reloads
the 16 heads' q (32 KB/block) for nothing plus more segments to add in the merge kernel. **That adaptive formula itself was right before the change; what was wrong was only that
the key count fed to it was a quantity that differed between the two paths** (`topk = min(cap, ng)`, where ng is "the number of groups completed up to the end of this batch").
The correct fix: the formula unchanged to the word, feed it `min(topk, (p+1)/ratio)` —— p is **this query's own** absolute position, independent of how many
tokens are in the batch, and identical, query by query, to what pure decode computes at the same position. The host opens the grid by the maximum segment count across queries, and the segment length is computed inside the kernel
(the extra segments of earlier queries take the empty-segment branch, which is exactly neutral for the merge: scores pressed to -inf ⇒ p=0, and when a whole segment is empty max=-1e30 in the merge times exp(-1e30−m)=0).

**★Two pits that led me into a ditch, worth more than the conclusion★**

1. **The gate script's false divergence**: speculation produces per round, so the last round spits out a few extra tokens, and the two outputs are different lengths. When comparing the "common prefix",
   the shorter one's last byte is the closing newline, while the longer one has the next token's first character at the same position —— `cmp -n min(length)`
   reports a divergence at the **last byte** of the common prefix. Two extra rounds of hunting for a "second source of cross-track divergence" were wasted on this, while the per-token id sequence was in fact completely identical.
   ⇒ the comparison must drop one more byte; to judge same-track it is best to compare directly the token id sequence printed by `--emit-trace`.
2. **The expert kernel's `order` parameter must be a template parameter**: after writing it as the runtime `order ? order[blockIdx.y] : blockIdx.y`,
   **the decode n=1 path (order=NULL) also became 21% slower** —— per-kernel table: gateup 8.20 → 9.95 ms/step, down 4.88 → 5.92,
   the whole step 47.2 → 50.1 ms, while the output was byte-unchanged. This kernel's 1024 threads × 64 registers + 64 KB codebook already saturates one SM,
   and one more possibility that "the pair may come from global memory" changed the whole kernel's compilation. After templating, the ORD=0 version is instruction-for-instruction identical to the pre-change one.
   ★The companion★: `cudaFuncSetAttribute` must be set for **both template instances**; miss one and that path quietly falls back to "codebook via global gather" (a 1.60 t/s-class collapse, with no error).

**M3′ the drafter (succeeded)**: the three towers' 7.3 GiB was originally last in load priority, with 3.28 GiB going through host mapping repeatedly reclaimed by kswapd,
while the draft reads it every round. Changed so that **when speculation is armed the three towers go ahead of the trunk experts** (the same level is not enough —— mtp.* is appended by the converter at the end of the file,
and within the same priority it still sorts last by offset), plus the flat copy built only for n=1 (freeing 3.5 GiB).
Reading: host mapping **3.28 → 2.45 GiB**, draft **23.9 → 13.5 ms/round (−44%)**.

| **now** | **47.8 ms** | **20.92** | **116.3 ms** | **13.5** | **102.5** | 1.86 | **15.22** |

★**The verify batch's 102.5 ms is speculation's only roadblock**★: pure decode is only 47.8 ms per step, while a round produces only 1.86 tokens.
The draft half is already cured (13.5 ms); the rest is all on the single item "verifying 3 positions costs 2.1× verifying 1" —— by bytes it should cost only 1.8×

### ★★09-17 mtp-1.md close-out: the remaining three segments done —— M4′/M6′ both negative verdicts (both with mechanism), M5′ scheduler landed★★

The user ordered "finish the remaining plan". The three segments, one by one.

**M4′ expert union: negative verdict, and this cut settles the matter**

On paper it was the biggest single item on the whole speculative path: in the verify batch, 4 tokens × top-6 = 24 (token, expert) pairs contain only about 14 unique experts,
and the expert kernel takes **53%** of a 115 ms round (gateup 38.5 + down 23.0 ms/round = **4.7×** the 13.0 ms single-token step),
while by bytes it should be only 2.4×. First tried the light one ("sort by expert id, so a duplicate's second read hits L2") —— the multiple did not budge from 4.7:
one pair needs 36 blocks, and between the two reads there is 40 MB of traffic, so the 24 MB L2 was long since flushed.
Then wrote a real dedup kernel (one block handles 2 pairs of the same expert, reads the bitstream once, looks up the codebook once, does the dot product twice, bit-identical):

| Dedup version's shape | codebook traffic | bitstream | activation | expert kernel one round |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| active (per-pair) | 110 MB | 53 MB | 1× | 61.5 ms |
| one block 32 rows | **+19 MB** | −41% | +17% | 105.6 (whole round) — no speedup |
| one block 64 rows | −42% | −41% | +17% | **60.5 ms (1.6%)** |

★Conclusion★: **cutting the bitstream by four tenths is useless, and cutting the codebook by four tenths is useless too** ⇒ this kernel's cost is neither the weight bytes nor the codebook traffic,
but **the work on each (index, token) pair itself** (one 16 B random table lookup + 8 element multiply-adds + one 16 B activation read).
What dedup saves is "how many times each index looks up the table"; it cannot save "every token must be multiplied against this row once".
Together with those three 09-16 negative verdicts on bitstream read methods, this is the fourth of the same root —— **do not come at it from the "read fewer bytes" direction again**.
The code was withdrawn; the negative-verdict archive went into `cuda_vq_decode.inc.cu`. The two remaining paths are both out of this round's scope: change the quantization format (quality line) / put the dot product on tensor cores.
★A valuable pit was also hit along the way★: the first version of the dedup kernel wrote the gain as `acc × (row gain × 反修 gain)`, whereas the active one is
`(acc × row gain) × 反修 gain` —— only down carries the 反修 gain, so every row differed by one rounding bit, the verify batch's argmax changed with it, and
the acceptance rate "rose" from 0.86 to 1.17. **It looked like an improvement, but it actually broke same-track** (the gate caught it at 2K byte 25).

**M5′ confidence scheduling: landed (`src/core/core_draft_sched.c`)**

The number of positions verified per round is no longer pinned at 3; it is set by the confidence the drafter reports itself:
a_j = ∏_{i≤j} sigmoid(conf_i) is the prefix survival rate when position j is reached, and k = argmax (1+Σ_{j≤k}a_j) / cost(k) is chosen.
The cost uses ratios "with one pure decode step as 1" (c_draft 0.285 / c_fix 0.615 / c_tok 0.385, all three numbers measured on disk).
★Does not learn the wall clock online★: k is determined only by conf and compile-time constants ⇒ at temp 0 the same input gives the same k (and changing k does not change the output anyway, speculation is same-track).
When the predicted value < 1 (not even the draft cost is earned back), it rests 16 rounds before trying again; the probing overhead amortizes to 1.8%.
**Its correct behavior on this base is "most of the time it produces no draft"** —— c_tok = 0.385 means that below an acceptance rate of 0.67 speculation loses money,
and the measured p1 is only around 0.5. After changing the base (smaller experts or the dot product on tensor cores), re-weigh those three numbers and speculation turns on by itself.

**M6′ drafter alignment: changed the metric, still a negative verdict —— this family can be closed**

That 09-16 attempt aligned hidden states with pure L2; the negative verdict's diagnosis was "the objective function is wrong: the argmax is determined by the fine differences in the exit head's 12.9 × 10⁴ rows,
while L2 spends its effort on the high-variance directions". This round, following that diagnosis, changed to the **exit metric**: while capturing, the engine additionally computes on the GPU the per-column sum of squares of the exit head
W[V][D] (new kernel `v41_head_colnorm_kernel`, written to `<pairs>.hdiag`), the solver whitens by diag(WᵀW)
(`dspark_align --hdiag`), and after solving divides A's columns back.

| | verify residual (uncorrected = 1.0) | ★first-position agreement rate (the verdict)★ |
|---|---:|---:|
| not attached | 1.000 | **0.5604** |
| pure L2 (09-16) | 0.56 | 0.4336 |
| **exit metric diag(WᵀW)** | **0.5148** | **0.4111** |

(8191 positions captured, first 2048 rows for fit/verify, λ=1 K=512.)
★Both times the same signature: the quantity being fit halved, while the real criterion dropped instead.★ So the problem is not in the metric's precision ——
**"linearly bend the drafter's exit hidden state onto the main model's" as a family does not hold**: the drafter is not a noisy version of the main model,
it is a different function, and the residual is the main signal; the hidden state obtained after fitting away half the residual is neither the drafter's nor the main model's, and the
argmax is worse than either end. Raising the acceptance rate leaves only "retrain the drafter", and that is beyond this round's scope (iron rule: the goal is weight-space restoration, zero training).
★The tools stay in the repo★: `--hdiag` and `--rows` (the row-space solve is O(n²·D), and 8191 rows simply killed the process, so by default only the first 2048 rows are used).

**★09-17 close-out gate (all green)★** `speed-bench/d1_kv_ring_gate.sh` against HEAD's ds4.base, same run same machine state:

| Scenario | self-consistency | byte vs baseline | same-track | new t/s | baseline t/s |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| 2K pure decode | ✓ | ✓ | — | 20.02 | 20.01 |
| 12k pure decode | ✓ | ✓ | — | 19.83 | 19.96 |
| 2K speculative (`--dspark`) | ✓ | — | ✓ | 18.84 | — |
| 12k speculative (`--dspark`) | ✓ | — | ✓ | 17.14 | — |

The scheduler rested 3/4 times in each of the two scenarios (16 rounds each), and a round dropped from 116 to 97 ms (it narrowed k from 3 to 2 by itself).
**Speculation went from "25% slower" to "6% slower"**, and the default is off ⇒ the active path is pure decode at 20 t/s, byte-identical to before the change and on par in speed.

★The final account of this round★: speculation cannot win on this base, because of a computable inequality ——
one round's cost = draft 0.285 + verify(1+k) = 0.615 + 0.385(1+k) (with one pure decode step as 1); to win, the
acceptance rate must be p1 > 0.67, while the measured value is only 0.50~0.56. And the two movable numerator and denominator both got negative verdicts:
c_tok 0.385 cannot come down (M4′: cutting bytes by four tenths is worth only 1.6%), p1 cannot go up (M6′: both metrics made the real criterion drop instead).
⇒ **For speculation to turn around, the base must be changed first** —— the expert path reads fewer weights per token (change the quantization format), or that dot product moves onto tensor cores.
Both are outside this round's scope, but the conclusion carries its mechanism, and the next person does not have to try from scratch.

## 2026-09-17 Speculation: the towers' quantization is real (worth 1 point), the grouped FP8 kernel has a real bug, and for the first time speculation beats single-stream at 12k

The user pointed it out at the 09-16 close-out: "the measurement is wrong, because the draft is the original model, but now it is a quantized model". Verified true ——
the three towers in the original HF are **F8_E4M3 + 32×32 block scaling**, while the quantization directory compressed them together with the base into FP4 1×32,
and the converter merely passed it straight through. The tower backbone is only ~260 MB in total, and restoring to FP8 adds only 129 MB (117.886 → 118.015 GB), a negligible cost.

### What was done
1. **The converter gains a second source** (`v41_to_gguf.c`'s 5th argument = the original HF directory): `mtp.*` is always taken from the original file and stored at native precision ——
   the five attention projections / the three shared-expert pieces / main_proj stored as FP8 (GGUF type 44), the routing gate / the two markov pieces / confidence stored as BF16.
2. **The engine dispatches by registered type** (`v41_tproj` / `v41_tproj_grouped` / `v41_small_matmul`): the old GGUF still runs, taking the fp4 path.
3. FP8 GEMV gains a `grid.y` group offset (the towers' wo_a is 8-group block-diagonal), and the `in_dim` multiple-of-512 requirement is relaxed to 32 (the towers' wq_b is 1280).

### Two pits (both "no error, only bad numbers")
- **norm stored as BF16 = straight garbage**: `v41_rms_norm_kernel` reads the weight as **f32** (`cuda_model_range_ptr(..., dim*4)`),
  and stored as BF16 it is still interpreted as f32. First-position agreement rate 0.5604 → **0.035**. norm always goes f32; only matrices that pass through the "dispatch by type" path may be stored BF16.
- **The grouped GEMV's output hard-coded `out_dim`**: in the kernel `out[t*out_dim + r]`, while the grouped call's `out_stride` (8192) ≠ `out_dim` (1024) ——
  the towers run B rows at a time, so **row 2 onward was all written into other groups' cells**. Agreement rate 0.5604 → 0.4302 (not thoroughly broken, the hardest kind to find).
  Adding the `out_stride` argument changed the signature but this spot was missed; for non-grouped calls out_stride == out_dim, so the old path was always right.

### The numbers (same ruler: finj 8192 positions teacher-forced, `dspark_agree`)
| | towers FP4 (before) | towers FP8 (after) |
|---|---:|---:|
| ① drafter ↔ deployed base | 0.5604 | **0.5707** |
| ② deployed base ↔ FP anchor | 0.6356 | 0.6356 (bit-unchanged ✓ the trunk was not touched) |
| ③ drafter ↔ FP anchor | 0.5023 | 0.5082 |

**The towers' quantization loss = 1.0 point.** Right direction, wrong magnitude —— restoring the towers' precision alone does not buy speculation's winning move.

### Speed gate (`d1_kv_ring_gate.sh none <new GGUF> 64 gate`, all green)
| Scenario | pure decode | speculative | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 2K English | 20.05 | 18.72 | −6.6%; acceptance 0.73/5, one round 94.8 ms produces 1.73 tokens |
| 12k English | 19.29 | **20.01** | **+3.7% —— for the first time speculation beats single-stream**; acceptance 1.20/5, one round 99.7 ms produces 2.20 tokens |
Same-track byte-identical ✓ self-consistency two runs same ✓ pure decode 20.05 matches before the change (the trunk was untouched).

**Why 12k wins and 2K loses**: the longer the context, the more expensive each pure decode token (attention grows with key count), while the verify batch spreads that attention over
1+k rows; and in a long context the next word is easier to guess (acceptance 0.73 → 1.20). **This trend says speculation's battlefield is the long context, not the short prompt.**

### The account: how far off (2K, at k=1)
Pure decode 49.9 ms/token. One round = draft 13.3 + verify (1+1 rows) 69.3 = 82.6 ms producing 1.57 tokens ⇒ 52.6 ms/token.
**Only 4.3 ms off** —— it is not "the acceptance rate must reach 0.8"; another tenth must be squeezed out of the draft's 13.3 ms or the verify's marginal 19.4 ms/token.
On the 12k side, of the verify's 85.8 ms, the per-query indexer (scoring + top-k ≈ 6.8 ms/query) takes ~11 ms ⇒ this is exactly the plan's
**M7 (long-context verify batch: read K together, only one extra q per query)** cell, and now it has measured backing.

### M7 negative verdict: the long-context verify batch's indexer cannot be saved by the approach the plan wrote (2026-09-17)
The plan's basis for M7 was the 09-16 old account "at 12k, topk 5.9 + scoring 0.9 ms/query". **That money was already spent on 09-16 itself by
two other cuts** (the scoring kernel changed to a grid.y group dimension, block selection changed to radix select). Today, same machine same ruler, per-kernel re-measurement (12k, 50000-character README):

| Kernel | pure decode ms/step | speculative (incl. verify batch) ms/step |
|---|---:|---:|
| `v41_indexer_score_kernel` | 0.72 | 0.79 |
| `v41_topk_kernel` | 0.26 | 0.21 |
| `v41_fp4x32_gemv_kernel` (backbone) | 19.65 | 17.34 |
| `v41_vq_gateup_kernel` | 8.48 | 12.49 |
| `v41_vq_down_kernel` | 4.97 | 6.41 |

The step-by-step timeline shows it even more definitively (same log, steps 44~51): pure decode step gateup 9.4 / down 5.3 / idx 0.7;
**the n=5 verify step gateup 55.8 / down 24.3 / idx 3.3**. ⇒ Of the ~65 ms by which the verify batch exceeds pure decode,
**the expert kernel accounts for 65 ms, the indexer only 2.7 ms**. Even done perfectly, M7 is worth only 2.7%.

**And it cannot be done**: the plan imagined "read K together, only one extra q per query". But the scoring kernel's cost is not reading K ——
the index keys are only ~210 KB across the whole model (L2-resident); the cost is **the dot product of those 64 heads on each (query, group) + 320 shuffle reductions**,
and 5 queries are 5 real jobs. **This is the same mechanism as M4′ (expert union)'s negative verdict**: saving "how many times it is read" is useless; it cannot save "every token must be multiplied once".
⇒ M7 stops, reason booked. Every one of the plan mtp-1.md's M0′~M7 now has a verdict.

### The only lever left (with measured backing, but it touches the quality line)
The verify batch's marginal cost = **16.3 ms/token, all in the VQ expert kernel** (at n=5, gateup+down 80.1 ms vs pure decode 14.7, near-linear).
And this kernel **at n=1 also only reaches ~123 GB/s** (the backbone kernel is already 178~198), so tensor-core-izing it is a double win: pure decode about 1.5×,
and the verify batch's marginal drops from linear to near the byte bound. **The cost**: the accumulation order changes ⇒ the output changes bitwise ⇒ it must pass the NLL ruler + five metrics, decided by the quality line, pending approval.
Another safe zone is the drafter itself (13.5 ms/round, 1.45 GB ⇒ ~107 GB/s, 2× off the wall) —— changing the drafter does not affect the output (verify backstops it),
but it is worth at most 6 ms/round.

**Default stays off**: 12k +3.7% is not a "substantial improvement" (user order 2026-09-16).

   the official +60~85% was measured in a multi-user batch (all 384 experts are read every step anyway, and the draft positions ride along for free). The same union kernel is worth 4× aggregate throughput in a multi-user batch.

The user ordered "execute". Following the order in mtp-2.md §9, the record up to segment A's speed gate.

  ⇒ **the tensor cores take f16, not TF32** (TF32 is unconditionally exact but halves throughput and doubles instructions).
  ★The pit hit★: the first version had the activation (x) and the intermediate (h) share one accumulator and one call counter ⇒ the printed line's **label was the last call's and the
  number was the sum of both**. A probe that lies to itself is worse than no probe; changed to two sets of counters.
- `[mtp-uniq]` (the draft towers' expert overlap, `core_v41_forward.c` factored out into `v41_moe_uniq_probe` shared by both sides):
  **of 15 pairs only 6.67 unique experts (44%)**, while the trunk verify batch is 17.4/24 (72%). The reason is that positions 1..4 in the block consume the same noise embedding,
  so the routing is nearly identical ⇒ the mtp-2 §6.1 cut (tower expert union) has more meat than estimated, and can save 56% of the tower expert arithmetic.
- `d0a_decode_profile.sh` gains three things: the `specno` profile (the speculative path but without nsys sampling, producing numbers in seconds), the third ncu pass (issue slots / instruction count / pipe saturation /
  shared conflicts), and ④ a per-kernel table classified by step type (draft / verify n= / prefill), plus a 10th argument `--dspark-verify N`.

**Segment A's kernel (new files `src/cuda/cuda_vq_tc_frag.inc.cu` + `cuda_vq_tc_moe.inc.cu`)**
Shape: grid(row/128, group slot), block = 8 row tiles (16 rows) × KSEG K segments; one block handles **one expert**, and the tokens in the batch that selected it
are the N dimension's 8 columns of `mma.m16n8k16.f16`; KSEG is set by the matrix shape (the largest divisor of nblk ≤ 4: gateup 4, down 3), **independent of how many tokens are in the batch**
⇒ same-track holds constructively. The codebook f16 goes straight into the A tile (weights unconditionally exact), activations bf16→f16 (mantissa lossless, range guarded by the watchdog).
The exit/clamp/SwiGLU/gain multiplication order is a verbatim identical formula to the active kernel; the reduce still uses the active one's single launch.

**Gates ①② passed**: `-Xptxas -v` **zero spill** (gateup 60 / down 72 registers); **element-wise cross-check** against the active scalar kernel
`max|new−old| = 2.892e-03, max|old| = 8.973, relative 3.22e-04` —— a difference of only the accumulation order should be on the order of 1e-4~1e-5, while a wrong fragment mapping would be above 1e-2.
(The error source is clear: the bf16 rounding at the gateup exit amplifies the accumulation-order difference by one notch —— h off by one ulp is a relative 0.78%, and down accumulates 2304 terms
spread out to 1.6e-4. So this cut **does change the output** and needs one quality re-baseline.)

**Three kernel-shape iterations (each time ncu first, then change code)**
| Cut | basis | reading | verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| first version (A tile 4 `lds.b32`, bitstream two rows per lane) | — | gateup 9.05 / down 4.36 ms/step (n=1; active 8.51 / 4.99) | on par |
| A tile switched to `ldmatrix.x4` | ncu: the primary stall became **mio_throttle 14.7~19.4** (active 0.3~2.0), i.e. "memory instructions cannot be issued"; the A tile's 64 of the total 152 instructions are 42% | instructions 152 → 62 per block/lane; registers 64→60 / 80→72; **the cross-check values not a word different** | ✓ |

The real cause of the bitstream's negative verdict: shared cannot hold the whole bitstream block (after the 64 KB codebook + 16.9 KB activations only 19 KB is left, while a whole block needs 26.6 KB), so it can only be loaded by half blocks
⇒ each block's `__syncthreads` goes from 2 to 4, and the cost of 1024 threads × 40 whole-block syncs exceeds the wavefronts saved.
To take this path again, intra-segment synchronization must come first (named barrier `bar.sync ks+1, 256` waiting only for this segment's 8 warps). The negative-verdict archive is already in the code.

global queueing saved is exchanged for shared loading + intra-segment synchronization + shared reads, for a net of zero.

**④ The markov head's "bounded-pruning exact argmax": the bound is too loose, not one candidate was pruned**
Per-position greedy reads the whole [129280][256] bf16 table (66 MB) for each position to compute the full-vocabulary bias; one round of 5 positions is 0.33 GB, measured 1.33 ms and **already at the bandwidth wall**
(248 GB/s) ⇒ the only option is to read fewer bytes. Using |bias_v| ≤ ‖W_v‖·‖e‖ to prune the words that cannot take the crown (the candidate set must contain the true argmax, it is not an approximation),
after writing it, the measured **candidates 129280 / 129280**, the draft instead 13.2 → 15.9 ms. Real cause: the markov table's rows are **nearly orthogonal** to embed,
so Cauchy-Schwarz is looser than logits' whole dynamic range, and every word's upper bound exceeds the winner's lower bound. The code was withdrawn, archived in ds4_gpu_v41.h.

**⑤ Two numbers still on the table unused** (measured by M0)
- `[mtp-uniq]`: the draft towers **have only 6.67 unique experts out of 15 pairs (44%)**, while the trunk verify batch is 72% —— positions 1..4 in the block consume the same noise embedding,
  so the routing is nearly identical. ⇒ The tower expert union can save 56% of the tower expert arithmetic (draft 4.43 → ~2.0 ms), affects speculation only, and this cut was not made.
- `[f16-range]`: of the activations/intermediates, 2100 × 10⁴ elements **overflow 0** (subnormal 0.22%) ⇒ when f16 tensor cores come later, the range is safe and there is no need to fall back to TF32.

### ★09-17 night re-review case opened: the VQ expert kernel only reaches half the wall, and it is not a shape ceiling, it is **not enough bitstream bytes in flight** (latency-limited)★

The user ordered: a day of zero progress, re-examine it, give a plan. Review only, no code changed. Conclusion: all seven negative verdicts changed "how to read each round"; not once was
**"issue the load several rounds ahead"** taken as a variable, and that is exactly the only cause.

**Evidence (all numbers already in the repo, not one newly measured)**
1. ncu (09-17 §2 table): primary stall long_scoreboard 15~25 (waiting on global data), issue slots 24~35%, L1 34~48%, LSU 24~34%,
   FMA 8~15% —— **not a single pipe is over half**. Every pipe is idle while the warp waits on data; that is the classic picture of "not enough requests in flight", not a "shape ceiling".
2. Little's law: 240 GB/s × on-board loaded latency ~1.5~2 µs ⇒ the whole card needs 360~480 KB in flight. The current kernel's bitstream is only 48 B per warp per round,
   `unroll 4` + a 64-register hard cap (1024 threads/block) ⇒ effectively only 1~2 rounds ahead ⇒ 48~96 B/warp × 1536 warp = **74~150 KB**
   ⇒ equivalent to **~110~130 GB/s**, exactly the measured 110~121.
3. `mem_ceiling.cu ④` is precisely this kernel's row-stream shape (a private row per warp, a thousand-odd concurrent warps), and only because the loads have no dependencies between them and the compiler issues deep,
   it reaches **237~241** ⇒ the DRAM side has no problem with this access pattern; the shortfall is entirely that the SM side does not issue deep enough.
4. Counter-evidence: 09-16 "two aligned reads + funnelshift" was 32% slower —— a three-way branch by itself is not worth three tenths; the branch pins the load behind the branch,
   the cross-round hoist is gone, and in-flight drops from ~2 rounds to 1. **Consistent with the MLP hypothesis, not with the "instruction count" hypothesis.** Likewise 09-16's
   "4 byte reads fall in the same sector, not waiting on memory at all" was misjudged: each bitstream byte is read only once in the whole run, so the first read each round is a DRAM miss and the warp waits on it every round.
5. The dedup kernel (bytes −41%) is not faster, the tensor-core kernel (instructions −57%) is not faster, lg_throttle 22~27% (narrow loads fill the queue while bytes do not go up) —— all different faces of the same disease.

**The plan** (two steps, the first falsified in 10 minutes; byte-identical throughout, gate = cmp)
- Step 0 probe: in the active kernel `v41_vq_row_dot`'s loop add `prefetch.global.L2` pointing at the bitstream address of round k+8, one instruction, changing no arithmetic.
  Expected gateup 8.3 → 5.5~6 ms/step; **if not a millisecond moves ⇒ the hypothesis is wrong, stop immediately**.
- Step 1 the real thing: the bitstream, per round, is read by lane 0..11 each taking one **aligned 32-bit word** (8 B load alignment already verified: the first load's offset after the slot table is 9232, gate/up are
  2,035,736 B each, down 2,041,880 B, the bitstream start is 8-aligned, and the tail is padded with 8 zero bytes), a register ring of D=8~16 slots **issued D rounds ahead**, and those D rounds at the row's end
  instead issue the next row's first D words (row-to-row pipelining); each lane needs two shfl to get words a and a+1 (a=⌊3·lane/8⌋, exactly 8 lanes straddle words, and a+1≤11 always stays inside the block)
  + funnelshift + and. The lane↔index mapping, the accumulation chain, and the reduction tree are not changed by a word. The NK (20/8) template is dispatched by nidx_row/32, changing only `v41_vq_row_dot`.
  Criterion: ncu long_scoreboard 15~25 → <5, expert kernel 13.3 → 7~8 ms/step, single token 48.3 → ~42.5 ms (≈23.5 t/s).
- Step 2 (do it only if step 1 stops at ~180 GB/s): at load time transpose the bitstream on the device side into "30 B contiguous per lane" (the file is untouched), ~2.5 instructions per index, zero shfl;
  the prefill dequant read method goes with it, not touched for now.

baseline = the 09-17 night `ds4` copied to `ds4.base_pf`; every version `cmp`-checked for temp 0 output):

| Version | gateup ms/step | down | whole-step median | t/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline | 8.25 | 4.92 | 47.9 | 20.88 |
| step 0 probe: whole row one row ahead `prefetch.global.L2` (line-wise / sector-wise the two versions are the same) | 7.12 | 4.64 | 46.5 | 21.53 |
| cut ①: bitstream as 384 B whole blocks (3 whole-line LDG.32) into registers + two shfl distributes per round | 7.06 | 4.51 | 45.8 | 21.81 |
| cut ②③: cross-block software pipelining (issue the next block / next row's first block before computing this one) + the 8 codebook loads issued together + down 4 rows/warp | **6.72** | **3.76** | **45.2** | **22.10** |

**What the new ruler said** (`gguf-tools/bench/mem_ceiling.cu` ⑤⑥, measured for the first time):
- Single-hop latency: L1 18 ns / L2 143 ns / DRAM 377 ns (2.42 GHz).
- The "private row per warp, 48 B per round" stream: **in flight 1/2/4/8/16 rounds all give 135~142 GB/s**, and adding `ld.global.L2::128B/256B` hints does nothing ⇒ the re-review case's
  "latency depth" hypothesis is **wrong**. 64 B per round ⇒ 187~207, **128 B whole line ⇒ 219** (wall 237~241). ⇒ Real cause: **request granularity**, DRAM fetches in 64 B units, so half of the 48 B is fetched for nothing.
- Prefetching the row's first 30 sectors together: only reaches 224 with concurrent rows (D=4), 134 for a single row (D=1) —— unreliable, so the kernel relies not on prefetch but on whole-line reads.
- The real cause of the three bitstream read methods' negative verdicts (09-16) is here too: all three versions were still 48 B per round.

**ncu (after cut ①, gateup, n=1)**: global load sectors 11.2 M/launch (activations 16 sectors/round are seven tenths of it), L1 wavefronts 10.4 M (of which shared codebook table lookups 5.74 M = 11.7/round,
bank conflicts 3.5 M = 61%; LDS.128 makes one wavefront per 8 lanes, and 8 random lanes land in 8 bank groups ⇒ expected max multiplicity ~2.9 × 4 = 11.7 ✓),
long_scoreboard **17~18 is still the primary stall**, mio/lg <1, L1 throughput 36~48%, LSU 23~30%, FMA 12~16%. ⇒ The basis for cut ②: after three syncs per block, 32 warps
lockstep-wait on the block read, and the SM and DRAM take turns idling. In SASS, 60 `LDG.E.U8` are all `v41_vq_open`'s memcpy of header fields (once per block), not on the hot path.

**Geometry re-scan** (after cuts ②③): gateup 2 rows/warp 6.72 < 4 rows 7.19 < 8 rows 8.77 —— the fewer blocks, the slower, monotonically; 8 rows = 48 block = exactly 1 wave,
the cheapest on paper (codebook traffic 4× less, no tail) is measured the slowest ⇒ 1 wave has no load balancing, and the whole launch waits for the slowest SM. down 4 rows (240 block = 5 wave) 3.76.

**The four follow-up escalations afterward all got negative verdicts (same ruler, all byte-identical), archived**:
| Cut | gateup / down ms/step | why |
|---|---:|---|
| activations loaded one round ahead into registers | 6.74 / 4.07 | the activation LDG is an L1 hit (ncu's fifth pass: L1 sector hit 81%), not a source of waiting; 4 more registers hit the 64 hard cap and hurt instead |
| two-level queue two blocks ahead (across rows and stages by block sequence) | 7.40 / 3.90 | 30~40 more bookkeeping instructions per block + 6 registers |
| `__launch_bounds__(1024,1)` + row gain hoisted to the row start | 7.11 / 3.90 | ptxas fills all 64, and the same algorithm becomes slower instead; falling naturally to 56/48 is faster |
| round count as a template parameter (straight-line code)  | — | MID=**2304** (not 2048): down is 9 rounds per row, the tail block 1 round; 72 registers, 1024 threads do not fit the SM, launch fails |
★The ruler's jitter★: the same code (56/48 registers) over two runs gives gateup 6.72 vs 7.19, down 3.76 vs 3.72, whole step 45.2 vs 45.4 ⇒ **±0.3~0.5 ms per kernel is run-to-run noise**,
so the differences among 6.72/7.06/7.19 above cannot be taken at face value; only two cuts hold up: bitstream whole-block read 8.25 → ~7.1, down pipelining + 4 rows/warp 4.92 → ~3.8.

| **16 warp/block (512 threads, occupancy 33%)** | **10.28 / 5.03** | 1.4× slower, not 2× and not 1× ⇒ half is L1TEX queueing (shrinks with warp count), half is each warp's own chain |
⇒ ★The expert kernel has reached its floor in the "each lane does one 16 B codebook lookup per index" structure★: 16 L1TEX wavefronts per round (codebook lookups 11.7 = the expected max multiplicity 2.9 × 4 quarter-warps
for 8 random lanes landing in 8 bank groups; activations 4) + 32 warps lockstep queueing + the 64-register hard cap. Final version = whole-block read + one block ahead + down 4 rows +

### ★09-18 case opened: the decode whole-step CUDA graph —— one capture, replay with the position in a device slot (user order "execute the biggest single mine, 6.4 ms")★

**The target**: 12k's one step is 45.7 ms = kernel-busy 39.5 + gaps 4.5 (~1500 launches/step) + the step boundary's 3 synchronized cudaMemcpy + engram waiting on pread.
After graph the gap target is ~0.5 ms; small-kernel fusion (mHC/rms/rope 3.9 → 1.5) is the next cut, and it only pays off once graph has landed.

**Why not "re-capture every step + ExecUpdate" (the llama.cpp way)**: in the V4 era, the 09-07 measurement had the host overhead push the round gap from 3.8 to 12.3 ms, a net loss
(archived in cuda_graphcap.inc.cu); ExecUpdate over 1500 nodes + argument upload is 3~5 ms of host time every step, which can only be hidden with ping-pong pipelining, a complex machine that
still eats CPU. The correct fix = **capture the graph once, and each step change only the {token, position} in the device slot**, making the host's per-step work ≈ write the slot + one cudaGraphLaunch.

**The design (no value change, gate = temp 0 byte-identical + graph byte-identical to --no-graph)**
1. The position `pos0` changes from "kernel argument" to "device slot": treat the st->pos tensor (rope already reads it) as posd, and the relevant kernels gain `const int32_t *posd`
   (NULL = the old basis, prefill/direct-dispatch paths not changed by a word). When posd is non-NULL the kernel computes it itself: ng = (pos+1)/ratio, topk = min(TOPK, ng),
   vis = ng, ring slot = (pos+i) % window. Involved: indexer scoring/candidate blocks/topk, sparse attention (the mma decode version + the merge kernel),
   win_commit, the compression source layer (a new "append + pool when full" kernel launch, replacing two host-offset memcpy + conditional pooling), the two pack kernels
   (group ids computed on the device; when a group is not full it writes into a **garbage slot** at the end of the cache that is never read —— so this chain launches unconditionally every step, and the graph topology is independent of the phase).
2. The grid is capped by **bucket**: position bucket 1024 per cell, and within a bucket ng_cap/nseg_cap are fixed (surplus blocks of the scoring kernel run empty; attention empty segments return immediately,
   and the merge kernel computes the true segment count from posd itself and reads only true segments —— it writes no zeros and reads no zeros, bit-identical). Re-capture across buckets (once per 1024 token, tens of ms).
3. engram's disk read: inside the graph, before the engram layer place a **host node** (cudaLaunchHostFunc, captured as a node) waiting for the thread pool's pread to finish,
   followed by a pinned → device memcpy node. So the whole step is still one graph, while pread still overlaps with the GPU computation of the preceding layers.
4. Step boundary: {tok, pos, pre_mix one-hot} go through pinned slots + memcpy nodes (replacing 3 synchronized cudaMemcpy); at the graph's end an argmax kernel +
   a 4 B D2H node; after the host sync it reads the slot → emit → writes the next step's slot → launches again.
5. The first decode step goes by direct dispatch (warming all lazy allocations: flat copy/staging/mma attributes), and capture starts from the second step. Prefill, speculation, and the prof/dump/hook paths do not enter the graph.
6. CLI `--no-graph` (for diagnostic A/B); named by mechanism (decode graph), without a version name.

**The gates to pass**: 2K/12k temp 0 byte-identical to ds4 (the final VQ kernel); the same binary's graph vs --no-graph byte-identical; self-consistency two runs same;
across-bucket (2K prompt generating 64 steps crossing the 2048 boundary) same; `make linecount` green.

**Landed (compiled into spark's ds4 at 09-18 05:22, kept as ds4.graph1)**: new files `src/cuda/cuda_decode_graph.inc.cu` (capture/instantiate/launch/host node/
pinned async copy) + `src/core/core_decode_graph.c` (orchestration: buckets, slots, capture, direct-dispatch restart, closed-form advancing of the host counters); the three indexer pieces split out into
`cuda_v41_indexer.inc.cu` (v41_2 hit 500 lines); the position basis enters the kernels: scoring/candidates/topk/attention mma decode version + merge kernel/win_commit/two pack kernels
(garbage slot)/the new compress_step launch (append + pool when full); the engram row buffer becomes permanently pinned + a graph-internal host node waiting for pread; `--no-graph` is only for A/B.
One step, one graph is **1496 nodes** (including cuBLAS's 80-launch amplifier Sgemm, ThreadLocal capture passes straight through).

**Gate (d1_kv_ring_gate.sh graph mode, 64 steps, mtpnative + zchain)**: all green ——

| **graph path** | **41.7** | 39.7 | **2.1** | **24.0** |
⇒ the graph took 3.6 ms/step (−8%); kernel-busy did not move a word (the same set of kernels). The per-kernel totals are the same on both sides (gemv 19.1 / gateup 7.1 / down 3.8 / attn 2.0 / …).
**The composition of the remaining 2.1 ms (awk scanning the 30-step timeline, pairing each gap with the kernels around it)**: the gap between nodes inside the graph is only **~0.1 µs each** (39761 gaps of ≤2 µs sum to 0.14 ms/step ——
graph scheduling itself is nearly seamless, so PDL and the like are unnecessary); the holes are in two places: ① `hc_post(L0) → ?` **1.33 ms/step** (1 of them) = the host node before the engram layer waiting on pread;

costs 170 µs, 80× more than a 2 µs small kernel; ③ the step boundary `? → embed` 53 µs (host sync + emit + write slot + launch).
**Two cuts**: replace all the memcpy nodes with zero-copy small kernels (the kernel uses `__ldcv` to read mapped pinned memory directly / the argmax result is written back to mapped memory by a small kernel; the same for
engram's two 6 KB uploads); add timing to the engram wait (submit→complete / real wait) to pin the cause down.
**The result of the zero-copy cut**: 12k wall clock 41.7 → 42.1 (within the noise), gaps still 2.2 —— those 4 × 172 µs are not the memcpy nodes themselves; it is the **step boundary** mixed in
(the one from the D2H node to the next graph's first H2D node at ~650 µs plus the three real memcpys at ~10 µs each average out to 172). The zero-copy small kernels stay (no loss, 4 fewer node types).
**Host-side breakdown (2K, 127 steps on the graph, new timing)**: from the previous step's sync returning to this step entering is **304 µs** (= emit: writing the token text via fwrite+fflush to the file) / startup + row-fetch submit
**131 µs** (broadcast waking 48 threads) / **cudaGraphLaunch is only 39 µs** (1496 nodes, not a problem) / waiting on the graph 40.2 ms.
**engram (decode step, recording n=1 only)**: row-fetch task submit→complete **2.62 ms**; 1.22 ms from graph launch to the host node (= L0 + callback latency); real wait **1.24 ms/step**.
⇒ The two holes' real causes: ① one round of pread is 2.6 ms (48 threads × 2 reads of 4 KB O_DIRECT) and cannot hide inside L0's 1.2 ms; ② the step boundary 0.6 ms = emit + row-fetch submit + wake.
Cuts: ① a ruler for the disk (gguf-tools/bench/pread_lat.c) to first separate "the disk is slow" from "threads/queueing are slow", then decide whether io_uring one-shot submit or something else; ② change the loop to "launch the next step's
graph first, then emit the current token" (both emit and row-fetch submit hide inside GPU time).
**The disk ruler (spark NVMe, the engram table = hf shards 47/48, 4 KB O_DIRECT random reads)**: single read **median 200 µs** (p90 200~300, tail 0.7~9.6 ms);
48 threads × 2 (= the engine's original shape) one round averages 1.79 ms / best 1.10; 96 × 1 one round 2.45; 16 × 6 one round 1.53; 1 × 96 serial 27.5 ms (287 µs each).
⇒ The disk's concurrency floor = one round of 96 reads at 1.1~1.5 ms, even longer than L0's 1.2 ms —— "read both layers in one round" can never be hidden; the engine's 2.6 adds to this two **serial** reads
per thread + the wake.
**The cut (already landed)**: row fetching is split into rounds by engram layer —— round 0 reads only the L1 layer (24 rows = 48 single reads, with the unit split by "one pread": half 0 reads the weight 256 B, half 1 reads
the scale 8 B, one read per 48 threads ≈ one disk latency), and as soon as it is collected the round for the L14 layer is issued (there is 13 ms of margin before L14); each engram layer in the graph gets one host node before it.
The loop becomes launch first, then emit, then wait (emit's 300 µs hides inside the graph's run time).
**The result of round-splitting + launch-before-emit (build 3)**: the step boundary 654 → 165 µs ✓; but 12k's wall clock is still 41.7 and the gap still 2.2 —— each of the two host nodes leaves a hole of **0.94 ms**,
while round 0's real wait is only 0.58 and round 1's is 0: ★**a host node itself costs 0.6~0.9 ms on GB10** (waking the driver's callback thread + pushing the following nodes up after the callback returns),
independent of whether it waited for anything★. Round 0's pread is still 2.1 ms (48 threads thundering herd: woken together by the condition variable, fighting over one lock together), while the disk ruler says 48 parallel single reads need only ~0.25 ms
(under 48-way QD, NVMe completes ~230 reads per millisecond).
**build 4: host nodes replaced by a GPU spin kernel** (a 1-thread small kernel `__ldcv`-polling the pinned flag flag[ei] ≥ want, and the host's v41_engram_graph_serve sets one layer as each is collected;
on a 5 s timeout it writes err and lets it through, checked after the host sync) —— 2K 128 steps: **40.9 ms/step (24.28 t/s)**, output byte-identical to the previous version; engram's round 0 is still 2.2 ms ⇒ before L1
there is still ~0.7 ms of stall. 12k nsys per-node: **gaps 2.2 → 1.3 ms**, engram's hole is gone (the two spin kernels together wait only 0.20 ms/step); the remaining 1.17 ms is
the step boundary caused by nsys slowing the host calls (under sampling, row-fetch submit 1.3 ms and cudaGraphLaunch 1.4 ms; without sampling 154 + 36 µs), not the engine's account ——
★under nsys the wall clock is from now on only about the gap composition; the steady-state per-step wall clock is the engine's own `[graph] … steady X ms/step` (= sync→enter + startup + launch + wait on graph)★:
2K 127 steps = 0.001 + 0.154 + 0.036 + 39.76 = **39.95 ms/step (25.0 t/s)** (the engine's decode 5.2 s/127 = 40.9 includes the first step's direct dispatch + one capture of ~130 ms). **build 5: io_uring row fetching** (core_v41_ering.c, raw system calls, the main thread computes hashes, one submit for the whole round of 48 O_DIRECT reads, a queue of 512
with prefill continuing in batches; falls back to the thread pool on non-Linux or if it cannot open) —— target round 0 ~0.3 ms, zero stall before L1.
Measured: round 0 submit→complete **0.97 ms** (2.2 → 0.97), 2K steady state 0 + 137 + 29 + 38560 = **38.7 ms/step (25.8 t/s)**; ★but the gate went red★: 12k's direct path already diverged from the baseline at
the 1st byte, and the two graph-path runs disagreed —— the **io_uring landing-slot reuse bug**: the first version chose the landing slot by i % queue length and kept issuing as long as in-flight was below the queue length, but completions are
out of order, so during a prefill round of 24576 reads, request i+512 would overwrite the same landing slot before request i had landed (a decode round of 48 was fine; the prefill's rows got corrupted).
Fix: strict batching —— the next batch is issued only after the previous batch is fully collected, and the landing slot = the index within the batch (build 6, passing the gate together with the four small-kernel fusions).
**The lesson**: the "two runs disagree" cell (self-consistency) is the first red light to come on, and it separates "a data race" from "the values changed" with one stroke —— the gate must keep the self-consistency cell.
